title: Equilibrium of Concurrent Forces & Free Body Diagrams: Pulleys, Strings & Atwood Machine
description: Condition of equilibrium for concurrent forces (Σ F⃗ = 0), Lami's theorem, systematic step-by-step Free Body Diagram (FBD) methodology, tension in strings, and Atwood machine dynamics.
syllabus_pacing: Mid-Term Examination | Unit III: Laws of Motion
subtopics: Definition of Concurrent Forces: Forces whose lines of action pass through a common point
Equilibrium condition: Vector sum of concurrent forces is zero (Σ F⃗ = 0)
Resolution into components: Σ F_x = 0, Σ F_y = 0, Σ F_z = 0
Lami's Theorem for three coplanar concurrent forces in equilibrium: P/sin α = Q/sin β = R/sin γ
Systematic protocol for drawing Free Body Diagrams (FBD): Isolating bodies, identifying contact/field forces
Ideal strings and pulleys: Light (massless), inextensible, frictionless (uniform tension T)
Atwood Machine analysis: Acceleration a = (m₁ - m₂)g / (m₁ + m₂) and Tension T = 2 m₁ m₂ g / (m₁ + m₂)
key_concepts: Atwood Machine Acceleration and Tension Formulas
success_criteria: Isolate any component in a mechanical system and draw its complete, accurate FBD
Apply Lami's theorem to solve three-force equilibrium hanging rope problems
Derive acceleration and string tension for connected blocks and pulley systems
Resolve concurrent forces along mutually perpendicular axes to set up equilibrium equations
chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 4: LAWS OF MOTION
## MODULE 4: Equilibrium & Free Body Diagrams

### 1. Equilibrium of Concurrent Forces
Forces are said to be **concurrent** if their lines of action intersect at a common point.
A particle is in **equilibrium** under concurrent forces if the vector sum of all forces is zero:
$$\sum \vec{F} = \vec{F}_1 + \vec{F}_2 + \dots + \vec{F}_n = \vec{0}$$
In Cartesian components:
$$\sum F_x = 0, \quad \sum F_y = 0, \quad \sum F_z = 0$$

### 2. Lami's Theorem
For three concurrent coplanar forces $\vec{P}, \vec{Q}, \vec{R}$ in equilibrium:
$$\frac{P}{\sin \alpha} = \frac{Q}{\sin \beta} = \frac{R}{\sin \gamma}$$
where $\alpha$ is the angle between $\vec{Q}$ and $\vec{R}$, $\beta$ is the angle between $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{R}$, and $\gamma$ is the angle between $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$.

### 3. Atwood Machine (Two Masses Connected over a Pulley)
Two masses $m_1 > m_2$ connected by a light inextensible string over a frictionless pulley:
- For mass $m_1$ moving downwards:
  $$m_1 g - T = m_1 a \quad \text{--- (1)}$$
- For mass $m_2$ moving upwards:
  $$T - m_2 g = m_2 a \quad \text{--- (2)}$$
Adding (1) and (2):
$$(m_1 - m_2) g = (m_1 + m_2) a \implies a = \left(\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) g$$
Substituting $a$ into (2):
$$T = \left(\frac{2 m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) g$$

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 4.6: See Fig. 4.8. A mass of 6 kg is suspended by a rope of length 2 m from the ceiling. A force of 50 N in the horizontal direction is applied at the mid-point P of the rope, as shown. What is the angle the rope makes with the vertical in equilibrium? (Take g = 10 m s⁻²). Neglect the mass of the rope.
worked_examples.given: m = 6 kg, F = 50 N horizontal, g = 10 m/s², rope length = 2 m.
worked_examples.formula: T₁ cos θ = W = mg; T₁ sin θ = F = 50 N.
worked_examples.substitution: T₁ cos θ = 6 kg × 10 m/s² = 60 N; T₁ sin θ = 50 N. Dividing: tan θ = (T₁ sin θ)/(T₁ cos θ) = 50 / 60 = 5/6.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The angle made by the rope with the vertical is approximately 40°.

common_misconceptions: Assuming string tension is equal to the hanging mass weight (T = mg) during acceleration: Tension equals mg ONLY when a = 0 (at rest). When accelerating, T = m(g - a) or T = m(g + a)!

title: Friction Mechanics: Static, Kinetic & Rolling Friction, Laws of Friction & Angle of Repose
description: Microscopic origins of friction, self-adjusting static friction, limiting friction, kinetic friction, laws of friction, angle of friction, angle of repose, and motion on rough inclined planes.
syllabus_pacing: Mid-Term Examination | Unit III: Laws of Motion
subtopics: Origin of friction: Microscopic interlocking of asperities and cold welds
Static Friction (f_s): A self-adjusting opposing force (0 <= f_s <= f_s,max)
Limiting Friction: Maximum static friction f_s,max = μ_s N
Kinetic (Dynamic) Friction: Friction during relative sliding f_k = μ_k N (μ_k < μ_s)
Graph of friction force vs applied force showing linear static phase, peak, and kinetic plateau
Laws of Friction: Independence of apparent contact area; proportionality to normal force
Angle of Friction (θ_f): Angle between resultant contact force and normal force (tan θ_f = μ_s)
Angle of Repose (α): Minimum tilt angle of inclined plane at which a body begins to slide (tan α = μ_s)
Rolling Friction: Origins (surface deformation) and why μ_r << μ_k (advantages of ball bearings)
key_concepts: Kinetic Friction f_k = μ_k N (μ_k < μ_s)
Angle of Repose Identity (tan α = μ_s)
success_criteria: Sketch the friction vs applied force curve and identify static, limiting, and kinetic regimes
Prove that the angle of repose is equal to the angle of friction
Calculate acceleration of a block sliding down a rough inclined plane: a = g(sin θ - μ_k cos θ)
Explain why pushing a lawnmower is harder than pulling it using FBDs
chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 4: LAWS OF MOTION
## MODULE 5: Friction Mechanics

### 1. Nature of Friction
Friction is the contact force parallel to the interface that opposes relative sliding between two surfaces.
- **Static Friction ($f_s$)**: Opposes the impending motion. It is **self-adjusting** in both magnitude and direction:
  $$f_s = F_{\text{applied}} \quad (\text{as long as body remains at rest})$$
  Maximum static friction is the **limiting friction**:
  $$f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N$$
  where $\mu_s$ is the coefficient of static friction and $N$ is normal force.
- **Kinetic Friction ($f_k$)**: Opposes actual relative sliding:
  $$f_k = \mu_k N$$
  Since fewer cold welds form during motion:
  $$\mu_k < \mu_s$$

### 2. Angle of Repose ($\alpha$)
The minimum angle of an inclined plane at which a body placed on it just begins to slide down by gravity:
Along the incline:
$$mg \sin \alpha = f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N$$
Perpendicular to incline:
$$N = mg \cos \alpha$$
Dividing:
$$\frac{mg \sin \alpha}{mg \cos \alpha} = \frac{\mu_s N}{N} \implies \tan \alpha = \mu_s$$
*Theorem*: Angle of repose is equal to the angle of friction!

### 3. Pushing vs. Pulling a Lawnmower
- **Pushing**: Applied force has a downward vertical component $\implies N = mg + F\sin\theta \implies$ Friction increases ($f_k = \mu_k(mg + F\sin\theta)$).
- **Pulling**: Applied force has an upward vertical component $\implies N = mg - F\sin\theta \implies$ Friction decreases ($f_k = \mu_k(mg - F\sin\theta)$).
*Conclusion*: **Pulling is always easier than pushing!**

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 4: LAWS OF MOTION
## MODULE 6: Dynamics of Circular Motion

### 1. Centripetal Force
Any motion along a curved circular path of radius $r$ requires an inward centripetal acceleration $a_c = v^2/r$. By Newton's second law, this requires a net inward **centripetal force**:
$$F_c = m a_c = \frac{m v^2}{r} = m \omega^2 r$$
Centripetal force is not an independent physical force; it must be provided by actual physical forces (tension in a string, gravity for satellite, friction for car).

### 2. Motion of a Car on a Level Road
On a flat horizontal circular road:
- Vertical: $N = mg$
- Horizontal: Static friction between tires and road provides centripetal force:
  $$f_s = \frac{m v^2}{r} \le f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg$$
$$\frac{m v^2}{r} \le \mu_s mg \implies v \le \sqrt{\mu_s r g}$$
$$\mathbf{v_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}}$$
If $v > v_{\text{max}}$, friction is insufficient and the car skids outward!

### 3. Banking of Roads
To avoid skidding on wet roads and reduce tire wear, the road is tilted inward at an angle $\theta$ (**banking**).
- **Optimum Speed (Zero Friction Condition)**:
  Tires experience no sideways frictional force. The horizontal component of normal reaction $N$ alone provides centripetal force:
  $$N \sin \theta = \frac{m v_0^2}{r}$$
  $$N \cos \theta = mg$$
  Dividing equations:
  $$\tan \theta = \frac{v_0^2}{r g} \implies \mathbf{v_0 = \sqrt{r g \tan \theta}}$$
- **Maximum Safe Speed with Friction ($\mu_s$)**:
  When driving faster than $v_0$, impending skid is outward $\implies$ friction $f_s$ acts down the incline:
  $$N \cos \theta - f_s \sin \theta = mg$$
  $$N \sin \theta + f_s \cos \theta = \frac{m v_{\text{max}}^2}{r}$$
  Setting $f_s = \mu_s N$ and solving:
  $$\mathbf{v_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{r g \left(\frac{\mu_s + \tan \theta}{1 - \mu_s \tan \theta}\right)}}$$

common_misconceptions: Thinking banking eliminates friction entirely: Banking provides an OPTIMUM speed v₀ at which friction is zero. At speeds higher or lower than v₀, friction acts to prevent skidding!

questions.question: Why are railway tracks banked on curved rails?
questions.ideal_answer: By raising the outer rail above the inner rail, the normal reaction from the rails is tilted inward. Its horizontal component provides the required centripetal force for the turn, preventing derailment and reducing wear on the wheel flanges.
questions.socratic_hint: What provides the centripetal force if the tracks are flat?

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 4: LAWS OF MOTION
## MODULE 7: Complete NCERT Exercise Solver

### Summary of Classical Problems
- **Apparent Weight of Man in Elevator of Mass $m$ (Exercise 4.14)**:
  - (a) Moving upward with uniform speed $v$: $a = 0 \implies N = mg$ (True weight).
  - (b) Accelerating downward with $a$: $mg - N = ma \implies N = m(g - a)$ (Weight decreases).
  - (c) Accelerating upward with $a$: $N - mg = ma \implies N = m(g + a)$ (Weight increases).
  - (d) Cable snaps (Free fall, $a = g$): $N = m(g - g) = 0$ (**Weightlessness**).

- **Helicopter Forces (Exercise 4.16)**:
  Mass of helicopter $M = 2000\text{ kg}$, crew/passengers $m = 500\text{ kg}$, upward acceleration $a = 15\text{ m/s}^2$:
  - (a) Force on floor by crew: $N = m(g + a) = 500(10 + 15) = 12,500\text{ N}$ downwards.
  - (b) Action of rotor on surrounding air: $F = (M + m)(g + a) = 2500(25) = 62,500\text{ N}$ downwards.
  - (c) Force on helicopter by surrounding air: Reaction to rotor force $= 62,500\text{ N}$ upwards.

worked_examples.problem: NCERT Exercise 4.14: A man of mass 70 kg stands on a weighing scale in a lift which is moving (a) upwards with a uniform speed of 10 m s⁻¹, (b) downwards with a uniform acceleration of 5 m s⁻², (c) upwards with a uniform acceleration of 5 m s⁻². What would be the readings on the scale in each case? (Take g = 10 m s⁻²). (d) What would be the reading if the lift mechanism failed and it hurtled down freely under gravity?
worked_examples.given: m = 70 kg, g = 10 m/s².
worked_examples.formula: (a) a = 0 => N = mg; (b) a = 5 m/s² down => N = m(g - a); (c) a = 5 m/s² up => N = m(g + a); (d) Free fall a = g => N = m(g - g) = 0.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) 70 kg; (b) 35 kg; (c) 105 kg; (d) 0 kg (State of weightlessness).

questions.question: What is the reading of a spring balance if the elevator cable breaks and the elevator falls freely?
questions.ideal_answer: Zero. Under free fall (a = g downwards), both the body and the spring balance fall with acceleration g; thus no restoring force develops in the spring and apparent weight is zero (weightlessness).
questions.socratic_hint: What is N when a = g in N = m(g - a)?

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 5: WORK, ENERGY AND POWER
## MODULE 1: Scalar Product & Work Done by Constant and Variable Forces

### 1. The Scalar (Dot) Product of Two Vectors
- **Definition**: The scalar product of two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, denoted by $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}$, is defined as the scalar quantity:
  $$\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = A B \cos \theta$$
  where $A = |\vec{A}|$, $B = |\vec{B}|$, and $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ ($0 \le \theta \le \pi$).
- **Properties**:
  1. **Commutative**: $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = \vec{B} \cdot \vec{A}$.
  2. **Distributive**: $\vec{A} \cdot (\vec{B} + \vec{C}) = \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} + \vec{A} \cdot \vec{C}$.
  3. **Orthogonal unit vectors**:
     $$\hat{i} \cdot \hat{i} = \hat{j} \cdot \hat{j} = \hat{k} \cdot \hat{k} = 1$$
     $$\hat{i} \cdot \hat{j} = \hat{j} \cdot \hat{k} = \hat{k} \cdot \hat{i} = 0$$
  4. **Component form**: If $\vec{A} = A_x \hat{i} + A_y \hat{j} + A_z \hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = B_x \hat{i} + B_y \hat{j} + B_z \hat{k}$:
     $$\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z$$
  5. **Angle between two vectors**:
     $$\cos \theta = \frac{\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}}{|\vec{A}| |\vec{B}|} = \frac{A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z}{\sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2} \sqrt{B_x^2 + B_y^2 + B_z^2}}$$

### 2. Definition & Classification of Work
- **Definition**: Work is said to be done by a force when the point of application of the force undergoes a displacement along or opposite to the line of action of the force.
  $$W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = F d \cos \theta$$
  - **SI Unit**: Joule (J), where $1\text{ J} = 1\text{ N}\cdot\text{m} = 1\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}$.
  - **Dimensions**: $[M L^2 T^{-2}]$.
- **Classification of Work**:
  1. **Positive Work** ($0 \le \theta < 90^\circ$): $\cos\theta > 0$. Example: Work done by gravitational force on a freely falling body.
  2. **Negative Work** ($90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$): $\cos\theta < 0$. Example: Work done by friction force on a sliding block ($W = f_k d \cos 180^\circ = -f_k d$).
  3. **Zero Work**:
     - When displacement $d = 0$ (e.g. pushing a rigid wall).
     - When force $F = 0$ (e.g. motion in deep space).
     - When $\theta = 90^\circ$ ($\vec{F} \perp \vec{d}$): Examples: Centripetal force in circular orbit ($W = \int \vec{F}_c \cdot d\vec{r} = 0$), coolie carrying a load horizontally on his head against vertical gravity ($W_g = mg d \cos 90^\circ = 0$).

### 3. Work Done by a Variable Force
- When force varies with position $F = F(x)$, we divide the displacement into infinitesimal intervals $\Delta x$:
  $$W = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \sum_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x) \Delta x = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x) dx$$
- In 3 dimensions:
  $$W = \int_{\vec{r}_i}^{\vec{r}_f} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F_x dx + \int_{y_i}^{y_f} F_y dy + \int_{z_i}^{z_f} F_z dz$$
- **Graphical Rule**: The work done by a variable force is geometrically equal to the **area under the $F-x$ curve** bounded by the displacement axis. Areas above the x-axis represent positive work; areas below represent negative work.

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 5.1: Find the angle between force F⃗ = (3î + 4ĵ - 5k̂) unit and displacement d⃗ = (5î + 4ĵ + 3k̂) unit. Also find the projection of F⃗ on d⃗.
worked_examples.formula: F⃗ · d⃗ = F_x d_x + F_y d_y + F_z d_z; cos θ = (F⃗ · d⃗) / (|F⃗| |d⃗|); Projection = F⃗ · d̂ = (F⃗ · d⃗) / |d⃗|.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The angle between the vectors is cos⁻¹(0.32) ≈ 71.3°, and the projection of F⃗ on d⃗ is 16/√50 ≈ 2.26 units.

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 5.2: It is well known that a raindrop falls under the influence of the downward gravitational force and the opposing resistive force of the air. The latter is known to be proportional to the speed of the drop but is otherwise undetermined. Consider a drop of mass 1.00 g falling from a height 1.00 km. It hits the ground with a speed of 50.0 m s⁻¹. (a) What is the work done by the gravitational force? (b) What is the work done by the unknown resistive force?
worked_examples.formula: (a) W_g = mgh; (b) ΔK = 1/2 m v_f² - 1/2 m v_i²; By Work-Energy Theorem: W_net = W_g + W_r = ΔK ⇒ W_r = ΔK - W_g.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Work done by gravity is +9.80 J. (b) Work done by the air resistive force is -8.55 J.

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 5.3: A cyclist comes to a skidding stop in 10 m. During this process, the force on the cycle due to the road is 200 N and is directly opposed to the motion. (a) How much work does the road do on the cycle? (b) How much work does the cycle do on the road?
worked_examples.given: F_road = 200 N opposite to motion, d = 10 m.
worked_examples.formula: W = F d cos θ.
worked_examples.substitution: (a) For the road on the cycle: θ = 180°. W_road = (200 N)(10 m) cos 180° = -2000 J. (b) For the cycle on the road: By Newton's third law, the cycle exerts an equal and opposite force of 200 N on the road in the direction of motion. However, the road does not undergo any displacement (d_road = 0).
worked_examples.calculation: (a) W_road = -2000 J = -2 kJ. (b) W_cycle = (200 N)(0 m) = 0 J.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) The road does -2000 J of work on the cycle (dissipating its kinetic energy into heat). (b) The cycle does zero work on the road because the road is stationary.

common_misconceptions: Confusing Newton's third law action-reaction pairs with work reciprocity: While the cycle exerts +200 N on the road, the road has zero displacement, so the work done by the cycle on the road is strictly zero, not +2000 J!

questions.question: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth. What is the work done by the gravitational force on the satellite in one complete revolution?
questions.ideal_answer: Zero. The gravitational force acts radially inward toward the Earth's center, perpendicular to the instantaneous tangential displacement of the satellite at every point along the circular orbit (θ = 90°). Thus dW = F_g · dr = F_g dr cos 90° = 0 at every instant!
questions.socratic_hint: What is the angle between the radial gravitational force and the tangential velocity vector?

Units and scalar nature of kinetic energy (strictly non-negative K ≥ 0)

Stopping distance and stopping time formulations derived from the Work-Energy Theorem

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 5: WORK, ENERGY AND POWER
## MODULE 2: Kinetic Energy & The Work-Energy Theorem

### 1. Kinetic Energy
- **Definition**: The kinetic energy of an object is a measure of the work an object can do by virtue of its motion.
  $$K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{2} m (\vec{v} \cdot \vec{v})$$
  - Since mass $m > 0$ and $v^2 \ge 0$, kinetic energy is **always a non-negative scalar quantity** ($K \ge 0$).
  - **Relation with Linear Momentum $p = mv$**:
    $$K = \frac{p^2}{2m} \implies p = \sqrt{2mK}$$

### 2. The Work-Energy Theorem for a Constant Force
- From the third equation of kinematics for rectilinear motion with constant acceleration $a$:
  $$v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s \implies a s = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2}$$
- Multiplying both sides by mass $m$:
  $$m a s = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 - \frac{1}{2} m u^2$$
- Since $F = ma$ and $W = F s$:
  $$W = K_f - K_i = \Delta K$$
- **Statement**: *The work done by the net force acting on a body is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.*

### 3. Proof of the Work-Energy Theorem for a Variable Force (Calculus Method)
- The instantaneous kinetic energy is $K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$.
- Differentiating $K$ with respect to time $t$:
  $$\frac{dK}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{1}{2} m v^2\right) = \frac{1}{2} m \left(2 v \frac{dv}{dt}\right) = m \frac{dv}{dt} v$$
- By Newton's second law, $F = m \frac{dv}{dt} = ma$:
  $$\frac{dK}{dt} = F v = F \frac{dx}{dt}$$
- Multiplying both sides by $dt$:
  $$dK = F dx$$
- Integrating both sides from initial state $(x_i, K_i)$ to final state $(x_f, K_f)$:
  $$\int_{K_i}^{K_f} dK = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F dx$$
  $$K_f - K_i = \int_{x_i}^{x_f} F dx = W$$
  $$\therefore W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$$
- **Crucial Rule**: The work-energy theorem holds for **all forces** acting on the particle — conservative, non-conservative, internal, and external!

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 5.4: A block of mass m = 1 kg, moving on a horizontal surface with speed v_i = 2 m s⁻¹ enters a rough patch ranging from x = 0.10 m to x = 2.01 m. The retarding force F_r on the block in this range is inversely proportional to x over this range: F_r = -k / x for 0.1 < x < 2.01 m, where k = 0.5 J. What is the final kinetic energy and speed v_f of the block as it crosses this patch?
worked_examples.given: m = 1 kg, v_i = 2 m/s, x_i = 0.1 m, x_f = 2.01 m, F_r = -k/x with k = 0.5 J.
worked_examples.formula: Work-Energy Theorem: K_f = K_i + W = 1/2 m v_i² + ∫_{x_i}^{x_f} F_r dx.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The final kinetic energy of the block is 0.5 J and its speed is 1.0 m s⁻¹.

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 5.5: A bullet of mass 0.012 kg and horizontal speed 70 m s⁻¹ strikes a block of wood of mass 0.4 kg and instantly comes to rest with respect to the block. The block is suspended from the ceiling by thin wire. Calculate the height to which the block rises. Also, estimate the amount of heat produced in the block.
worked_examples.formula: Conservation of linear momentum: m_1 u_1 = (m_1 + M) V; Energy conservation during swing: 1/2 (m_1 + M) V² = (m_1 + M) g h ⇒ h = V² / (2g); Heat produced = Initial KE - Final KE.
worked_examples.calculation: Heat produced ΔQ = 29.4 J - 0.86 J = 28.54 J.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The block rises to a height of 21.2 cm, and approximately 28.5 J of mechanical energy is dissipated as heat.

common_misconceptions: Assuming kinetic energy can be negative: Since kinetic energy depends on speed squared v², K is strictly non-negative. However, the *change* in kinetic energy ΔK can be negative if the object slows down.

questions.question: If the linear momentum of a body is increased by 50%, what is the percentage increase in its kinetic energy?
questions.ideal_answer: Let initial momentum be p, initial KE be K = p² / (2m). New momentum p' = 1.5p. New KE K' = (1.5p)² / (2m) = 2.25 [p² / (2m)] = 2.25 K. Percentage increase = [(K' - K)/K] × 100% = (2.25 - 1) × 100% = 125%!
questions.socratic_hint: Express kinetic energy as K = p² / 2m and substitute p' = 1.5 p.

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 5: WORK, ENERGY AND POWER
## MODULE 3: Potential Energy & Spring-Mass Systems

### 1. Potential Energy & Conservative Forces
- **Potential Energy ($U$)**: The energy stored in a body by virtue of its position, configuration, or state of strain in a force field.
  - Potential energy is only defined for **conservative forces**.
  - The change in potential energy $\Delta U$ is defined as the negative of work done by the conservative force:
    $$\Delta U = U_f - U_i = -W_c = -\int_{x_i}^{x_f} F_c(x) dx$$
- **Force as Negative Gradient of Potential Energy**:
  $$F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx}$$
  In 3D: $\vec{F} = -\nabla U = -\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\hat{k}\right)$.
- **Conservative Force Criteria**:
  1. The work done by the force in moving a particle between two points depends only on the initial and final positions, **not on the path taken**.
  2. The work done by the force around any closed path is zero: $\oint \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = 0$.
  - Examples: Gravitational force, electrostatic force, spring force.
  - Non-conservative examples: Friction, viscosity (path dependent, energy dissipated as heat).

### 2. Equilibrium Conditions on Potential Energy Curve $U(x)$
- At equilibrium, net force $F = 0 \implies \frac{dU}{dx} = 0$.
  1. **Stable Equilibrium**: $U(x)$ is a local minimum $\implies \frac{d^2 U}{dx^2} > 0$. Small displacements generate restoring forces back toward equilibrium.
  2. **Unstable Equilibrium**: $U(x)$ is a local maximum $\implies \frac{d^2 U}{dx^2} < 0$. Displacements cause the body to accelerate away.
  3. **Neutral Equilibrium**: $U(x)$ is constant $\implies \frac{d^2 U}{dx^2} = 0$.

### 3. The Spring Potential Energy & Mechanical Energy Conservation
- **Hooke's Law**: For an ideal massless spring, the restoring force exerted by the spring when stretched or compressed by displacement $x$ from natural length is:
  $$F_s = -k x$$
  where $k$ is the spring constant ($[k] = \text{N/m} = [M T^{-2}]$).
- **Work Done by Spring**:
  $$W_s = \int_0^{x_m} (-k x) dx = -\left[\frac{1}{2} k x^2\right]_0^{x_m} = -\frac{1}{2} k x_m^2$$
- **Spring Potential Energy**:
  $$U(x) = -W_s = \frac{1}{2} k x^2$$
- **Conservation of Mechanical Energy**:
  In an isolated system with only conservative forces:
  $$E = K + U = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \text{constant}$$
  - At maximum elongation $x = \pm x_m$: $v = 0 \implies E = \frac{1}{2} k x_m^2$.
  - At mean position $x = 0$: $U = 0 \implies E = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\max}^2$.
  - Maximum speed: $v_{\max} = x_m \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$.

The coefficient of friction between the block and the floor is μ = 0.2. Find the speed of the block when the spring returns to its uncompressed position (g = 10 m s⁻²).

worked_examples.finalAnswer: The speed of the block as it passes the uncompressed position is approximately 1.79 m s⁻¹.

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 5.7: A bob of mass m is suspended by a light string of length L. It is imparted a horizontal velocity v₀ at the lowest point A such that it completes a semi-circular trajectory in the vertical plane with the string becoming slack only on reaching the topmost point C. Obtain an expression for: (a) v₀; (b) the speeds at points B (horizontal) and C (topmost); (c) the ratio of kinetic energies (K_B / K_C) at B and C.
worked_examples.given: Mass m, string length L, lowest point A, horizontal point B, topmost point C.
worked_examples.formula: At top point C: Tension T_c ≥ 0 ⇒ mg = m v_c² / L ⇒ v_c = √(gL). Conservation of mechanical energy: E_A = E_B = E_C.
worked_examples.substitution: Taking lowest point A as potential energy datum (U_A = 0): E_A = 1/2 m v₀². At topmost point C (height h = 2L): E_C = 1/2 m v_c² + mg(2L) = 1/2 m (gL) + 2mgL = 5/2 mgL. Thus 1/2 m v₀² = 5/2 mgL ⇒ v₀ = √(5gL). At horizontal point B (height h = L): E_B = 1/2 m v_B² + mgL = 5/2 mgL ⇒ 1/2 m v_B² = 3/2 mgL ⇒ v_B = √(3gL).
worked_examples.calculation: K_B = 1/2 m v_B² = 3/2 mgL. K_C = 1/2 m v_c² = 1/2 mgL. Ratio K_B / K_C = (3/2 mgL) / (1/2 mgL) = 3.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) v₀ = √(5gL); (b) v_B = √(3gL), v_c = √(gL); (c) The ratio K_B / K_C = 3.

questions.question: A spring with spring constant k is cut into two equal halves. What is the spring constant of each half?
questions.ideal_answer: The spring constant of each half is 2k. Since spring constant is inversely proportional to spring length (k ∝ 1/L), halving the length doubles the stiffness!
questions.socratic_hint: Remember that k × L = constant for any elastic wire or spring.

title: Dynamics of Motion in a Vertical Circle & Engineering Mechanics of Power
description: Complete derivation of velocity, tension, and critical conditions for looping the loop in a vertical circle, definition of power as rate of energy transfer P = dW/dt = F⃗ · v⃗, units of power (Watt, Horsepower), and commercial electrical energy units (kWh).
syllabus_pacing: Mid-Term Examination | Unit IV: Work, Energy and Power
subtopics: Dynamics of non-uniform circular motion in a vertical plane
Tension equations at lowest point A, horizontal point B, and highest point C
Condition for completing the vertical circle without slacking: v_bottom ≥ √(5gR), v_top ≥ √(gR)
Tension difference between bottom and top points: T_bottom - T_top = 6 mg (universal constant)
Definition of Power: Average power P_avg = ΔW/Δt and Instantaneous power P = dW/dt
Force-Velocity formulation: P = dW/dt = (F⃗ · dr⃗)/dt = F⃗ · v⃗
Units of power: Watt (W = J/s), Kilowatt (kW), Horsepower (1 hp = 746 W)
Commercial unit of energy: Kilowatt-hour (1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J)
success_criteria: Derive the critical velocity at the lowest point required to complete a vertical circle: v = √(5gR)
Prove that the tension at the bottom exceeds the tension at the top by exactly six times the weight (6mg)
Calculate instantaneous power using the scalar product formula P = F v cos θ
Convert energy between Joules, kilowatt-hours, and electron-volts (eV)
chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 5: WORK, ENERGY AND POWER
## MODULE 4: Motion in a Vertical Circle & Power

### 1. Motion in a Vertical Circle
Consider a small body of mass $m$ tied to a string of length $R$ whirled in a vertical circle.
- At an arbitrary angle $\theta$ with the vertical downward direction:
  $$T - mg \cos \theta = \frac{m v^2}{R} \implies T = \frac{m v^2}{R} + mg \cos \theta$$
- **Condition to avoid string slacking at the highest point ($\theta = 180^\circ$)**:
  $$T_{\text{top}} = \frac{m v_{\text{top}}^2}{R} - mg \ge 0 \implies v_{\text{top}} \ge \sqrt{g R}$$
- **Speed at lowest point ($\theta = 0^\circ$) by conservation of mechanical energy**:
  $$\frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{bottom}}^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{top}}^2 + mg(2R)$$
  $$v_{\text{bottom}}^2 = g R + 4 g R = 5 g R \implies v_{\text{bottom}} \ge \sqrt{5 g R}$$
- **Speed at horizontal point ($\theta = 90^\circ$)**:
  $$v_{\text{mid}} = \sqrt{3 g R}$$
- **Tension Difference**:
  - $T_{\text{bottom}} = \frac{m(5gR)}{R} + mg = 6 mg$.
  - $T_{\text{top}} = \frac{m(gR)}{R} - mg = 0$.
  $$\Delta T = T_{\text{bottom}} - T_{\text{top}} = 6 mg$$

### 2. Definition & Formulations of Power
- **Power ($P$)**: The time rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
  - **Average Power**:
    $$P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}$$
  - **Instantaneous Power**:
    $$P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \frac{\vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r}}{dt} = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$$
- **Units**:
  - SI Unit: Watt (W), where $1\text{ W} = 1\text{ J/s} = 1\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-3}$.
  - Horsepower: $1\text{ hp} = 746\text{ W}$.
- **Electrical / Commercial Energy Unit**:
  - Kilowatt-hour (kWh):
    $$1\text{ kWh} = (1000\text{ W}) \times (3600\text{ s}) = 3.6 \times 10^6\text{ J}$$

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 5.8: An elevator can carry a maximum load of 1800 kg (elevator + passengers) moving up with a constant speed of 2 m s⁻¹. A frictional force of 4000 N opposes the motion. Determine the minimum power delivered by the motor to the elevator in watts as well as in horse power (g = 10 m s⁻²).
worked_examples.given: M = 1800 kg, v = 2 m/s (constant), f = 4000 N downward, g = 10 m/s².

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 5.9: A pump on the ground floor of a building can pump up water to fill a tank of volume 30 m³ in 15 min. If the tank is 40 m above the ground, and the efficiency of the pump is 30%, how much electric power is consumed by the pump? (Density of water = 10³ kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
worked_examples.formula: Mass of water m = ρ V; Output Work W_out = mgh; Output Power P_out = W_out / t; Input Power P_in = P_out / η.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The electric power consumed by the pump is approximately 43.6 kW.

common_misconceptions: Confusing power with energy: Power is the rate of energy consumption (Joules per second), while energy is the total accumulated work done (Power × Time). A 1000 W device running for 1 hour consumes 1 kWh of energy.

title: Collisions in One and Two Dimensions: Elastic, Inelastic & Coefficient of Restitution
description: Comprehensive analysis of elastic and inelastic collisions in 1D and 2D, conservation of linear momentum, kinetic energy conservation criteria, coefficient of restitution e, and complete velocity formulas for head-on collisions.
syllabus_pacing: Mid-Term Examination | Unit IV: Work, Energy and Power
subtopics: Definition of collision: Strong mutual interaction over a relatively short interval of time
Elastic collisions: Both linear momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
Inelastic collisions: Linear momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is converted into heat/sound
Perfectly inelastic collision: Colliding bodies stick together and move with a common velocity
Coefficient of restitution e = (v₂ - v₁) / (u₁ - u₂): e = 1 (elastic), 0 < e < 1 (inelastic), e = 0 (perfectly inelastic)
1D Head-on elastic collision velocity derivations: v₁ = [(m₁ - m₂)u₁ + 2m₂u₂] / (m₁ + m₂)
Special cases: Equal masses (complete velocity exchange), target at rest, heavy projectile vs light target
2D oblique elastic collision equations and glancing impact mechanics
key_concepts: Velocity Exchange in Identical Mass Collisions
Loss of Kinetic Energy in Perfectly Inelastic Collisions
success_criteria: State the conservation laws applicable to elastic and inelastic collisions
Derive the 1D elastic collision formulas for final velocities v₁ and v₂ from first principles
Prove that two identical masses exchange their velocities upon a head-on elastic collision
Calculate the kinetic energy loss in a perfectly inelastic collision: ΔK = 1/2 [m₁m₂ / (m₁ + m₂)] (u₁ - u₂)²
chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 5: WORK, ENERGY AND POWER
## MODULE 5: Collisions in 1D & 2D

### 1. Classification of Collisions
- **Collision**: An isolated event in which two or more colliding bodies exert relatively strong forces on each other over a short time.
- **Linear Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions** (since internal collision forces cancel in pairs by Newton's 3rd law and $\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0$).
  $$m_1 \vec{u}_1 + m_2 \vec{u}_2 = m_1 \vec{v}_1 + m_2 \vec{v}_2$$
- **Types of Collisions**:
  1. **Elastic Collision**: Linear momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved. No permanent deformation, no heat/sound generated.
  2. **Inelastic Collision**: Linear momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is NOT conserved (some KE converts into thermal, acoustic, or deformation energy).
  3. **Perfectly Inelastic Collision**: The two bodies stick together after impact and move with a single common final velocity ($v_1 = v_2 = V$). Maximum possible kinetic energy is lost!

### 2. Coefficient of Restitution ($e$)
- Defined as the ratio of relative velocity of separation to relative velocity of approach along the line of impact:
  $$e = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}$$
  - For perfectly elastic collision: $e = 1$.
  - For inelastic collision: $0 < e < 1$.
  - For perfectly inelastic collision: $e = 0$.

### 3. One-Dimensional Elastic Collision Derivation
Let two spheres of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ move with initial velocities $u_1$ and $u_2$ ($u_1 > u_2$) along the x-axis.
- By conservation of linear momentum:
  $$m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 \implies m_1(u_1 - v_1) = m_2(v_2 - u_2) \quad \text{--- (1)}$$
- By conservation of kinetic energy:
  $$\frac{1}{2} m_1 u_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 u_2^2 = \frac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 v_2^2 \implies m_1(u_1^2 - v_1^2) = m_2(v_2^2 - u_2^2) \quad \text{--- (2)}$$
- Dividing equation (2) by equation (1):
  $$u_1 + v_1 = v_2 + u_2 \implies u_1 - u_2 = v_2 - v_1$$
  *The relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation!* ($e = 1$).
- Solving for final velocities:
  $$v_1 = \left(\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_1 + \left(\frac{2 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_2$$
  $$v_2 = \left(\frac{2 m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_1 + \left(\frac{m_2 - m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_2$$
- **Crucial Special Cases**:
  1. **Equal Masses ($m_1 = m_2$)**:
     $$v_1 = u_2, \quad v_2 = u_1$$
     *The two colliding bodies completely exchange their velocities!*
  2. **Target initially at rest ($u_2 = 0$)**:
     $$v_1 = \left(\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_1, \quad v_2 = \left(\frac{2 m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\right) u_1$$
  3. **Massive projectile hitting tiny target ($m_1 \gg m_2, u_2 = 0$)**:
     $$v_1 \approx u_1, \quad v_2 \approx 2 u_1$$
  4. **Light projectile hitting massive stationary target ($m_1 \ll m_2, u_2 = 0$)**:
     $$v_1 \approx -u_1, \quad v_2 \approx 0$$

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 5.10: Consider the collision depicted in Fig. 5.10 to be between two billiard balls with equal masses m₁ = m₂. The first ball is called the cue ball and the second ball is called the target ball. The billiard player wants to 'sink' the target ball in a corner pocket which is at an angle θ₂ = 37°. Assume that the collision is elastic and that friction and rotational motion are not important. Obtain θ₁ (the scattering angle of the cue ball).
worked_examples.given: m₁ = m₂, u₂ = 0, elastic collision, θ₂ = 37°.
worked_examples.formula: Conservation of linear momentum: u⃗₁ = v⃗₁ + v⃗₂ ⇒ u₁² = v₁² + v₂² + 2 v₁ v₂ cos(θ₁ + θ₂); Conservation of KE: u₁² = v₁² + v₂².
worked_examples.substitution: Equating the two expressions for u₁²: v₁² + v₂² + 2 v₁ v₂ cos(θ₁ + θ₂) = v₁² + v₂² ⇒ 2 v₁ v₂ cos(θ₁ + θ₂) = 0. Since v₁ ≠ 0 and v₂ ≠ 0, cos(θ₁ + θ₂) = 0 ⇒ θ₁ + θ₂ = 90°.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The scattering angle of the cue ball is 53° (the two identical balls move at 90° relative to each other).

questions.question: In a nuclear reactor, fast neutrons (mass ≈ 1 u) are slowed down by colliding with moderator nuclei. Which moderator is more effective: Heavy nuclei (like Lead, 208 u) or Light nuclei (like Hydrogen, 1 u)?
questions.ideal_answer: Hydrogen nuclei (light water / heavy water). When a fast neutron collides head-on elastically with a proton (hydrogen nucleus of nearly identical mass m₁ ≈ m₂), they exchange velocities, reducing the neutron's speed almost to zero in a single collision! A collision with a heavy nucleus would cause the neutron to bounce back with nearly unchanged speed.
questions.socratic_hint: Recall the special case of elastic collisions when m₁ = m₂.

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 5: WORK, ENERGY AND POWER
## MODULE 6: Master NCERT Exercise Solver (Ex 5.1 to 5.24)

### NCERT Exercise Solutions Overview
This module contains complete, board-exam compliant solutions for all 24 exercise problems from NCERT Chapter 5: Work, Energy and Power.
- **Exercises 5.1 - 5.5**: Sign conventions of work, conservative versus non-conservative force distinctions.
- **Exercises 5.6 - 5.12**: Force-displacement integration, kinetic energy variations, and stopping distance proofs.
- **Exercises 5.13 - 5.18**: Industrial and everyday applications of power, mechanical efficiency, and kWh conversions.
- **Exercises 5.19 - 5.24**: 1D and 2D elastic/inelastic collisions, ballistic pendulums, and coefficient of restitution.

worked_examples.problem: NCERT Exercise 5.1: The sign of work done by a force on a body is important to understand. State carefully if the following quantities are positive or negative: (a) Work done by a man in lifting a bucket out of a well by means of a rope tied to the bucket. (b) Work done by gravitational force in the above case. (c) Work done by friction on a body sliding down an inclined plane. (d) Work done by an applied force on a body moving on a rough horizontal plane with uniform velocity. (e) Work done by the resistive force of air on a vibrating pendulum in bringing it to rest.
worked_examples.given: Five physical work interaction scenarios.
worked_examples.formula: W = F d cos θ: Positive if 0 ≤ θ < 90°, Negative if 90° < θ ≤ 180°.
worked_examples.substitution: (a) Applied force is upward and bucket displacement is upward (θ = 0°) ⇒ Positive. (b) Gravitational force is downward while bucket displacement is upward (θ = 180°) ⇒ Negative. (c) Friction acts upward along the incline while displacement is downward along the incline (θ = 180°) ⇒ Negative. (d) Applied force is in the direction of motion (θ = 0°) ⇒ Positive. (e) Air resistance acts opposite to velocity at every instant (θ = 180°) ⇒ Negative.
worked_examples.calculation: Signs: (a) Positive; (b) Negative; (c) Negative; (d) Positive; (e) Negative.

worked_examples.problem: NCERT Exercise 5.2: A body of mass 2 kg initially at rest is moved by a horizontal force of 7 N on a table with coefficient of kinetic friction = 0.1. Compute the: (a) Work done by the applied force in 10 s; (b) Work done by friction in 10 s; (c) Work done by the net force on the body in 10 s; (d) Change in kinetic energy of the body in 10 s, and interpret your results (take g = 9.8 m s⁻²).
worked_examples.formula: F_fric = μ_k mg; F_net = F_app - F_fric; a = F_net / m; s = 1/2 a t²; W = F · s.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) 882 J; (b) -247 J; (c) 635 J; (d) ΔK = 635 J. Notice W_net = ΔK, directly verifying the Work-Energy Theorem!

common_misconceptions: Thinking that total work done by applied force is equal to change in kinetic energy when friction is present: The Work-Energy Theorem states that NET work (including negative work done by friction) equals change in kinetic energy: W_applied + W_friction = ΔK.

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 6: SYSTEM OF PARTICLES AND ROTATIONAL MOTION
## MODULE 1: Center of Mass of Discrete and Continuous Systems

### 1. The Rigid Body Concept
- **Rigid Body**: An ideal body whose constituent particles remain at strictly invariant relative distances from each other regardless of applied external forces.
- **Types of Motion**:
  1. **Pure Translation**: Every particle of the body undergoes identical displacement in a given time interval. All particles have the exact same velocity $\vec{v}$ and acceleration $\vec{a}$ at every instant.
  2. **Pure Rotation**: The body rotates about a fixed axis; every particle moves in a circle whose center lies on the axis of rotation and whose radius equals the perpendicular distance from the axis.
  3. **General Plane Motion**: Combination of translation and rotation (e.g. a rolling bowling ball or wheel).

### 2. Center of Mass of a Two-Particle System
- Let two particles of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ be located along the x-axis at positions $x_1$ and $x_2$.
- The center of mass coordinate $X_{\text{cm}}$ is defined as:
  $$X_{\text{cm}} = \frac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2}{m_1 + m_2}$$
- **Key Geometric Invariant**: If the center of mass is taken as the origin ($X_{\text{cm}} = 0$):
  $$m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2 = 0 \implies m_1 r_1 = m_2 r_2 \implies \frac{r_1}{r_2} = \frac{m_2}{m_1}$$
  *The center of mass divides the line segment joining the two masses in the inverse ratio of their masses!* (Closer to the heavier mass).

### 3. Center of Mass of N Particles in 3 Dimensions
- For a system of $n$ particles with masses $m_1, m_2, \dots, m_n$ and position vectors $\vec{r}_1, \vec{r}_2, \dots, \vec{r}_n$:
  $$\vec{R}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n m_i \vec{r}_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n m_i} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \vec{r}_i$$
  where $M = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i$ is the total mass.
- In Cartesian components:
  $$X_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\sum m_i x_i}{M}, \quad Y_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\sum m_i y_i}{M}, \quad Z_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\sum m_i z_i}{M}$$

### 4. Continuous Mass Distribution
- For a continuous body, replace the summation by an integral:
  $$\vec{R}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{M} \int \vec{r} dm$$
- **Uniform Thin Rod of Length $L$ and Mass $M$**:
  - Linear mass density $\lambda = \frac{M}{L} \implies dm = \lambda dx = \frac{M}{L} dx$.
  - Taking one end at $x = 0$:
    $$X_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{M} \int_0^L x \left(\frac{M}{L} dx\right) = \frac{1}{L} \left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^L = \frac{1}{L} \cdot \frac{L^2}{2} = \frac{L}{2}$$
  - The center of mass lies exactly at its geometric midpoint!
- **Important Physical Invariant**: The center of mass need not lie inside the material of the body (e.g. hollow ring, hollow sphere, horseshoe magnet).

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 6.2: Find the centre of mass of a triangular lamina (equilateral or isosceles plate) of uniform mass density.
worked_examples.given: Uniform triangular lamina ABC.
worked_examples.formula: By symmetry, divide the triangle into narrow strips parallel to the base BC. The center of mass of each strip lies at its midpoint. The line joining the midpoints is the median from vertex A.
worked_examples.substitution: Similarly, dividing strips parallel to side AC shows the center of mass must lie along the median from vertex B. Therefore, the center of mass must lie at the intersection of the medians.
worked_examples.calculation: The intersection of the medians of a triangle is its centroid G.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The center of mass of a uniform triangular lamina coincides with its centroid G (which divides each median in the ratio 2:1 from the vertex).

common_misconceptions: Assuming center of mass must contain matter: For a hollow ring, doughnut, or hollow cylinder, the center of mass lies at the geometric center where no physical matter exists!

questions.question: Two bodies of masses 2 kg and 4 kg are separated by 6 m. How far is the center of mass from the 2 kg body?
questions.ideal_answer: 4 meters. By the inverse mass ratio rule, r₁ / r₂ = m₂ / m₁ = 4 / 2 = 2. Since r₁ + r₂ = 6 m, 2 r₂ + r₂ = 6 ⇒ 3 r₂ = 6 ⇒ r₂ = 2 m. Thus r₁ = 4 m from the 2 kg mass!
questions.socratic_hint: Use m₁ r₁ = m₂ r₂ where r₁ + r₂ = total distance.

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 6: SYSTEM OF PARTICLES AND ROTATIONAL MOTION
## MODULE 2: Motion of Center of Mass & Momentum Conservation

### 1. Velocity and Momentum of Center of Mass
- The position vector of the center of mass is:
  $$\vec{R}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \vec{r}_i$$
- Differentiating with respect to time $t$:
  $$\vec{V}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{d\vec{R}_{\text{cm}}}{dt} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \frac{d\vec{r}_i}{dt} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \vec{v}_i$$
- Multiplying by total mass $M$:
  $$M \vec{V}_{\text{cm}} = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \vec{v}_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \vec{p}_i = \vec{P}_{\text{total}}$$
- **Invariant**: *The total linear momentum of a system of particles is equal to the product of the total mass of the system and the velocity of its center of mass.*

### 2. Acceleration of Center of Mass & Newton's Second Law
- Differentiating $\vec{V}_{\text{cm}}$ with respect to time $t$:
  $$\vec{A}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{d\vec{V}_{\text{cm}}}{dt} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \frac{d\vec{v}_i}{dt} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \vec{a}_i$$
  $$M \vec{A}_{\text{cm}} = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i \vec{a}_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \vec{F}_i$$
- The total force on each particle $i$ consists of external forces $\vec{F}_i^{\text{ext}}$ and internal forces $\sum_{j \ne i} \vec{F}_{ij}^{\text{int}}$ exerted by other particles in the system:
  $$\sum_{i=1}^n \vec{F}_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \vec{F}_i^{\text{ext}} + \sum_{i \ne j} \vec{F}_{ij}^{\text{int}}$$
- By Newton's Third Law, $\vec{F}_{ij}^{\text{int}} = -\vec{F}_{ji}^{\text{int}}$ for every pair, so the internal force sum vanishes identically:
  $$\sum_{i \ne j} \vec{F}_{ij}^{\text{int}} = 0$$
  $$\therefore M \vec{A}_{\text{cm}} = \vec{F}_{\text{ext}}$$
- **Monumental Principle**: *The center of mass of a system of particles moves as if all the mass of the system were concentrated at that point and all external forces were applied directly at that point!* Internal forces cannot accelerate the center of mass!

### 3. Conservation of Linear Momentum of a System
- If the net external force acting on the system is zero ($\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0$):
  $$M \vec{A}_{\text{cm}} = 0 \implies \vec{A}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{d\vec{V}_{\text{cm}}}{dt} = 0 \implies \vec{V}_{\text{cm}} = \text{constant}$$
  $$\vec{P}_{\text{total}} = M \vec{V}_{\text{cm}} = \text{constant}$$
- **Physical Application: Exploding Projectile**:
  When a shell fired with initial velocity $\vec{v}_0$ explodes into fragments in mid-air due to internal explosive forces, $\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = M\vec{g}$ (gravity) is unchanged. Thus $\vec{A}_{\text{cm}} = \vec{g}$. The center of mass of the fragments continues moving on the identical parabolic trajectory as if no explosion had occurred!

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 6.3: A projectile of mass m is fired from the ground with speed v₀ at an angle θ with the horizontal. At the highest point of its trajectory, it explodes into two equal fragments. One fragment comes to rest immediately after the explosion and falls vertically downward. Where does the other fragment land with respect to the launch point?
worked_examples.given: Total mass m, launch speed v₀, launch angle θ, equal fragments m₁ = m/2, m₂ = m/2. Projectile explodes at peak x = R/2, y = H.
worked_examples.formula: Range R = (v₀² sin 2θ)/g; Since internal forces do not change the motion of the center of mass, the COM must land at x_cm = R. x_cm = (m₁ x₁ + m₂ x₂) / m.
worked_examples.substitution: Fragment 1 comes to rest at the peak, so it drops straight down and lands at x₁ = R/2. We have: R = [(m/2)(R/2) + (m/2) x₂] / m = 1/4 R + 1/2 x₂.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The second fragment lands at a distance of 1.5 R (or 3/2 of the original range) from the launch point.

common_misconceptions: Thinking that an explosion propels the center of mass: Chemical explosion forces are purely internal forces between the fragments. By Newton's 3rd law, they sum to zero and cannot change the acceleration of the center of mass!

questions.question: A man of mass 60 kg stands on a stationary wooden plank of mass 140 kg floating on a frictionless lake. If the man walks 4 m along the plank, how far does the plank shift relative to the shore?
questions.ideal_answer: 1.2 m backward. Since net external horizontal force F_ext = 0, the center of mass of the system remains stationary: m_man Δx_man + M_plank Δx_plank = 0. Let plank move backward by x: 60(4 - x) - 140(x) = 0 ⇒ 240 - 60x - 140x = 0 ⇒ 200x = 240 ⇒ x = 1.2 m!
questions.socratic_hint: Use the condition that ΔX_cm = 0 when F_ext = 0.

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 6: SYSTEM OF PARTICLES AND ROTATIONAL MOTION
## MODULE 3: Vector Product & Rotational Kinematics

### 1. The Vector (Cross) Product of Two Vectors
- **Definition**: The vector product of two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is defined as a vector $\vec{C} = \vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ whose magnitude is:
  $$|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = A B \sin \theta$$
  where $0 \le \theta \le \pi$ is the angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, and its direction $\hat{n}$ is perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ according to the **Right-Hand Thumb Rule**.
  $$\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = (A B \sin \theta) \hat{n}$$
- **Properties**:
  1. **Anti-commutative**: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$.
  2. **Collinear vectors**: If $\vec{A} \parallel \vec{B}$ ($\theta = 0$ or $\pi$), $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$. In particular, $\vec{A} \times \vec{A} = 0$.
  3. **Unit vectors**:
     $$\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k} \times \hat{k} = 0$$
     $$\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}, \quad \hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}, \quad \hat{k} \times \hat{i} = \hat{j}$$
     $$\hat{j} \times \hat{i} = -\hat{k}, \quad \hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i}, \quad \hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$$
  4. **Component Evaluation via Determinant**:
     $$\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ A_x & A_y & A_z \\ B_x & B_y & B_z \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(A_y B_z - A_z B_y) - \hat{j}(A_x B_z - A_z B_x) + \hat{k}(A_x B_y - A_y B_x)$$

### 2. Angular Velocity Vector & $\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$
- For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with angular velocity $\omega$, the vector $\vec{\omega}$ points along the axis of rotation in accordance with the right-hand rule.
- A particle at position $\vec{r}$ moves in a circle of radius $r_{\perp} = r \sin \theta$.
- Linear velocity magnitude: $v = \omega r_{\perp} = \omega r \sin \theta$.
- Since $\vec{v}$ is perpendicular to both $\vec{\omega}$ and $\vec{r}$:
  $$\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$$

### 3. Kinematic Equations for Rotational Motion with Constant Angular Acceleration
| Linear Kinematics (Constant $a$) | Rotational Kinematics (Constant $\alpha$) |
| :--- | :--- |
| $v = u + a t$ | $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$ |
| $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2$ | $\theta = \omega_0 t + \frac{1}{2} \alpha t^2$ |
| $v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s$ | $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2 \alpha \theta$ |
| $s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$ | $\theta_n = \omega_0 + \frac{\alpha}{2}(2n - 1)$ |

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 6.5: The angular speed of a motor wheel is increased from 1200 rpm to 3120 rpm in 16 seconds. (i) What is its angular acceleration, assuming the acceleration to be uniform? (ii) How many revolutions does the engine make during this time?
worked_examples.given: ω₀ = 1200 rpm, ω = 3120 rpm, t = 16 s.
worked_examples.formula: ω₀ = 2π × (1200/60) = 40π rad/s; ω = 2π × (3120/60) = 104π rad/s; α = (ω - ω₀) / t; θ = ω₀ t + 1/2 α t²; Revolutions N = θ / (2π).
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (i) Angular acceleration α = 4π rad s⁻² ≈ 12.6 rad s⁻²; (ii) The engine makes 576 revolutions.

common_misconceptions: Treating angular displacement as a true vector: Finite angular displacements do NOT commute (θ₁ + θ₂ ≠ θ₂ + θ₁), so finite rotations are NOT vectors! However, infinitesimal angular displacements dθ DO commute and are genuine vectors.

title: Torque, Angular Momentum of Particles and Systems & The Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum
description: Definition of torque τ⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗ as the turning effect of force, moment of a force, angular momentum of a particle L⃗ = r⃗ × p⃗, relation between torque and rate of change of angular momentum dL⃗/dt = τ⃗_ext, and conservation of angular momentum with real-world applications.
syllabus_pacing: Mid-Term Examination | Unit V: Motion of System of Particles and Rigid Body
subtopics: Torque (Moment of Force) definition: τ⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗ with SI unit N·m and dimensions [M L² T⁻²]
Magnitude of torque: τ = r F sin θ = F · (r sin θ) = Force × Perpendicular lever arm distance (d_⊥)
Sign convention of torque: Counter-clockwise torque is positive, clockwise torque is negative
Angular Momentum of a particle: L⃗ = r⃗ × p⃗ with SI unit J·s = kg·m²/s and dimensions [M L² T⁻²]
Relation between Torque and Angular Momentum: dL⃗/dt = d(r⃗ × p⃗)/dt = (dr⃗/dt × p⃗) + (r⃗ × dp⃗/dt) = (v⃗ × mv⃗) + (r⃗ × F⃗) = 0 + τ⃗ = τ⃗
Angular momentum of a system of particles: L⃗_total = Σ L⃗_i; dL⃗_total/dt = τ⃗_ext (internal torques cancel)
Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum: If τ⃗_ext = 0, L⃗ = constant ⇒ I₁ ω₁ = I₂ ω₂
Everyday illustrations: Figure skater/ballet dancer pulling in arms, springboard diver, planetary motion at perihelion/aphelion
key_concepts: Torque as Turning Effect: τ⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗
Rotational Newton's Second Law: τ⃗_ext = dL⃗/dt
Law of Conservation of Angular Momentum: I₁ ω₁ = I₂ ω₂

Prove the fundamental dynamic relation dL⃗/dt = τ⃗ from the definitions of L⃗ and p⃗
State the conditions for conservation of angular momentum and apply I₁ ω₁ = I₂ ω₂ to solve numericals
Explain why a spinning ballet dancer speeds up when she pulls her arms inward
chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 6: SYSTEM OF PARTICLES AND ROTATIONAL MOTION
## MODULE 4: Torque & Angular Momentum

### 1. Torque (Moment of Force)
- **Definition**: The turning or rotational effect of a force about a point or axis is called **torque** or **moment of force**.
  $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$$
- **Magnitude**:
  $$\tau = r F \sin \theta = F (r \sin \theta) = F \cdot d_{\perp}$$
  where $d_{\perp} = r \sin \theta$ is the **lever arm** (perpendicular distance from axis/origin to the line of action of force).
  - **SI Unit**: Newton-metre ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$).
  - **Dimensions**: $[M L^2 T^{-2}]$ (same dimensions as energy, but torque is a vector!).

### 2. Angular Momentum of a Particle
- **Definition**: The moment of linear momentum of a particle about a reference point is defined as its **angular momentum** $\vec{L}$:
  $$\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$$
- **Magnitude**:
  $$L = r p \sin \theta = m v (r \sin \theta) = m v r_{\perp}$$
  - **SI Unit**: Joule-second ($\text{J}\cdot\text{s} = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$).
  - **Dimensions**: $[M L^2 T^{-1}]$.

### 3. Relation Between Torque and Angular Momentum
- Differentiating $\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}$ with respect to time $t$:
  $$\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(\vec{r} \times \vec{p}) = \left(\frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \times \vec{p}\right) + \left(\vec{r} \times \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}\right)$$
- Since $\frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = \vec{v}$ and $\vec{p} = m \vec{v}$:
  $$\frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} \times \vec{p} = \vec{v} \times (m \vec{v}) = m (\vec{v} \times \vec{v}) = 0$$
- By Newton's second law, $\frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{F}$:
  $$\vec{r} \times \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = \vec{\tau}$$
  $$\therefore \vec{\tau} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt}$$
  *The time rate of change of angular momentum of a particle is equal to the torque acting on it.* (Rotational analogue of $\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$).

### 4. Conservation of Angular Momentum
- For a system of particles, internal torques cancel in pairs ($\sum \vec{\tau}_{\text{int}} = 0$):
  $$\frac{d\vec{L}_{\text{total}}}{dt} = \vec{\tau}_{\text{ext}}$$
- **Principle of Conservation of Angular Momentum**:
  *If the net external torque acting on a system is zero ($\vec{\tau}_{\text{ext}} = 0$), the total angular momentum of the system remains constant in magnitude and direction.*
  $$\vec{\tau}_{\text{ext}} = 0 \implies \vec{L}_{\text{total}} = \text{constant}$$
- Since $L = I \omega$:
  $$I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2$$
  - When moment of inertia $I$ decreases (e.g. ballerina pulling in arms), angular speed $\omega$ increases proportionally!

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 6.6: Show that the angular momentum about any point of a single particle moving with constant velocity remains constant throughout the motion.
worked_examples.given: A particle of mass m moves with constant velocity v⃗ along a straight line. Let O be any fixed origin.
worked_examples.formula: L⃗ = r⃗ × p⃗ = r⃗ × (m v⃗); Magnitude L = m v (r sin θ) = m v d_⊥.
worked_examples.substitution: Let d_⊥ be the perpendicular distance from origin O to the straight line of motion. As the particle travels along the line, the distance r and angle θ change, but the perpendicular distance d_⊥ = r sin θ remains strictly constant at all times.
worked_examples.calculation: Magnitude L = m v d_⊥ = constant. Direction of r⃗ × v⃗ is perpendicular to the plane containing O and the line of motion, which is also constant.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Since both magnitude (m v d_⊥) and direction are invariant, the angular momentum of a particle moving with constant velocity is strictly conserved about any chosen point.

common_misconceptions: Thinking that a straight-line moving body cannot have angular momentum: Angular momentum L = m v r_⊥ is defined about a point. As long as the line of motion does not pass through the reference origin (r_⊥ ≠ 0), a body moving in a straight line has non-zero angular momentum!

questions.question: A person sits on a rotating stool with weights held in outstretched hands. When he suddenly folds his hands, what happens to his angular velocity and kinetic energy?
questions.ideal_answer: Angular velocity increases because moment of inertia decreases and angular momentum L is conserved (I₁ ω₁ = I₂ ω₂). Rotational kinetic energy K = L² / (2I) INCREASES because I decreases! The extra kinetic energy comes from the biological internal muscular work done by the person in pulling the weights inward against centrifugal force.
questions.socratic_hint: Express kinetic energy in terms of angular momentum L and moment of inertia I.

title: Equilibrium of Rigid Bodies, Principle of Moments, Center of Gravity & Couples
description: Conditions for mechanical equilibrium of a rigid body (translational Σ F⃗ = 0 and rotational Σ τ⃗ = 0), principle of moments, mechanical advantage of levers, definition and distinction between Center of Gravity and Center of Mass, and mechanics of couples.
syllabus_pacing: Mid-Term Examination | Unit V: Motion of System of Particles and Rigid Body
subtopics: Conditions for mechanical equilibrium: Complete equilibrium requires both translational and rotational equilibrium
Translational equilibrium: Net external force is zero Σ F⃗_ext = 0 (linear momentum is constant)
Rotational equilibrium: Net external torque about any point is zero Σ τ⃗_ext = 0 (angular momentum is constant)
Partial equilibrium: A system in translational equilibrium but not rotational, or vice versa
Couple: A pair of equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide
Moment of a couple: τ_couple = Force × Arm of couple (independent of reference point)
Principle of Moments for levers: In equilibrium, Sum of anticlockwise moments = Sum of clockwise moments
Mechanical Advantage (MA) = Load / Effort = Effort arm / Load arm
Center of Gravity (CG): Point through which the resultant gravitational force (weight) acts
Equivalence and distinction between CG and CM (identical only in uniform gravitational fields)
key_concepts: Center of Gravity vs Center of Mass
success_criteria: Set up and solve simultaneous equations for both translational and rotational equilibrium
Calculate reaction forces at pivots and supports for loaded beams and inclined ladders
Define a couple and prove mathematically that its moment is independent of the point of calculation
Explain under what condition Center of Gravity fails to coincide with Center of Mass (huge celestial objects)
chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 6: SYSTEM OF PARTICLES AND ROTATIONAL MOTION
## MODULE 5: Equilibrium of Rigid Bodies & Principle of Moments

### 1. Conditions for Mechanical Equilibrium
A rigid body is in **complete mechanical equilibrium** if both its linear momentum and angular momentum are constant with time:
1. **Translational Equilibrium**: The vector sum of all external forces acting on the body must be zero:
   $$\sum_{i=1}^n \vec{F}_i = 0 \implies \sum F_x = 0, \quad \sum F_y = 0, \quad \sum F_z = 0$$
2. **Rotational Equilibrium**: The vector sum of all external torques acting on the body about any reference point must be zero:
   $$\sum_{i=1}^n \vec{\tau}_i = 0 \implies \sum \tau_x = 0, \quad \sum \tau_y = 0, \quad \sum \tau_z = 0$$

### 2. The Principle of Moments & Levers
- An ideal lever is a light rod pivoted at a point along its length called the **fulcrum** $F$.
- Let a load $W = F_1$ act at distance $d_1$ (load arm) and effort $P = F_2$ act at distance $d_2$ (effort arm) from the fulcrum.
- For rotational equilibrium about the fulcrum:
  $$\sum \tau = F_1 d_1 - F_2 d_2 = 0 \implies F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2$$
  $$\text{Load} \times \text{Load Arm} = \text{Effort} \times \text{Effort Arm}$$
- **Mechanical Advantage (MA)**:
  $$\text{MA} = \frac{\text{Load}}{\text{Effort}} = \frac{F_1}{F_2} = \frac{d_2}{d_1}$$
  If effort arm $d_2 > d_1$, $\text{MA} > 1$, and a small effort lifts a large load!

### 3. Couples
- **Couple**: A pair of equal and opposite forces acting along two parallel, non-coinciding lines of action.
- Examples: Turning a water tap, opening a bottle cap, turning a car steering wheel with two hands.
- **Key Theorem**: *The moment of a couple is independent of the reference origin.*
  $$\vec{\tau}_{\text{couple}} = \vec{r}_1 \times \vec{F}_1 + \vec{r}_2 \times \vec{F}_2 = \vec{r}_1 \times \vec{F} + \vec{r}_2 \times (-\vec{F}) = (\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2) \times \vec{F} = \vec{r}_{12} \times \vec{F}$$
  where $\vec{r}_{12}$ is the vector connecting the points of application. Magnitude $= F \times d_{\perp}$.

### 4. Center of Gravity vs. Center of Mass
- **Center of Mass (CM)**: Point determined solely by the mass distribution of the body ($\vec{R}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{1}{M}\int \vec{r} dm$). Independent of gravitational field.
- **Center of Gravity (CG)**: Point at which the total gravitational torque on the body vanishes: $\sum \vec{r}_i \times m_i \vec{g} = 0$.
- **When they coincide**: In a uniform gravitational field (where $\vec{g}$ is identical at all points of the body), CG coincides exactly with CM!
- **When they diverge**: For an extremely large body (e.g. a tall mountain or space elevator stretching thousands of kilometers into space where $\vec{g}$ varies with altitude), CG lies slightly below CM!

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 6.8: A 3 m long ladder weighing 20 kg leans on a frictionless wall. Its feet rest on the floor 1 m from the wall as shown in Fig. 6.8. Find the reaction forces of the wall and the floor.
worked_examples.given: Length L = 3 m, mass m = 20 kg ⇒ Weight W = mg = 20 × 9.8 = 196 N acting at midpoint of ladder (L/2 = 1.5 m). Distance from wall d = 1 m. Height of wall contact h = √(3² - 1²) = √8 = 2√2 ≈ 2.83 m. Wall is frictionless (normal reaction F₁ horizontal). Floor has friction: reaction F₂ has vertical component N and horizontal component f.
worked_examples.formula: Translational equilibrium: Σ F_x = 0 ⇒ F₁ = f; Σ F_y = 0 ⇒ N = W. Rotational equilibrium about bottom of ladder A: Σ τ_A = 0 ⇒ F₁ · h - W · (d/2) = 0.
worked_examples.substitution: N = W = 196 N. F₁ (2.83 m) - (196 N)(0.5 m) = 0 ⇒ 2.83 F₁ = 98 ⇒ F₁ = 98 / 2.83 ≈ 34.6 N. Horizontal friction at floor f = F₁ = 34.6 N.
worked_examples.calculation: Total reaction force of floor F₂ = √(N² + f²) = √(196² + 34.6²) = √(38416 + 1197) = √39613 ≈ 199 N. Angle with floor: tan θ = N / f = 196 / 34.6 ≈ 5.66 ⇒ θ ≈ 80°.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Reaction force of the wall is 34.6 N (horizontal); Reaction force of the floor is 199 N directed at 80° to the horizontal.

common_misconceptions: Assuming CG and CM are identical under all circumstances: While practically identical for laboratory scale objects, for massive bodies extending across non-uniform gravity fields, CG is pulled closer to the stronger gravitational field and sits below CM.

questions.question: Can a body be in translational equilibrium without being in rotational equilibrium?
questions.ideal_answer: Yes. A couple (two equal and opposite forces with parallel non-coinciding lines of action) has net force Σ F = 0 (translational equilibrium), but net torque Σ τ ≠ 0 (pure rotational acceleration). For example, turning a steering wheel with two hands!
questions.socratic_hint: Consider the net force and net torque produced by a couple.

description: Moment of inertia as rotational mass I = Σ m_i r_i² = ∫ r² dm, radius of gyration k, parallel and perpendicular axis theorems, standard moments of inertia for regular solids, and dynamics of pure rolling motion without slipping on horizontal and inclined planes.

subtopics: Moment of Inertia (Rotational Inertia): Definition I = Σ m_i r_i² with SI unit kg·m² and dimensions [M L² T⁰]
Physical meaning: Resistance of a body to rotational acceleration about a given axis (depends on mass, shape, and axis position)
Radius of Gyration k: Effective distance from axis where entire mass can be concentrated I = M k² ⇒ k = √(I/M)
Perpendicular Axis Theorem (for planar laminae): I_z = I_x + I_y
Parallel Axis Theorem: I = I_cm + M d²
Standard Moments of Inertia: Thin ring (MR²), Circular disc (1/2 MR²), Solid cylinder (1/2 MR²), Hollow cylinder (MR²), Solid sphere (2/5 MR²), Hollow sphere (2/3 MR²), Thin rod (1/12 ML²)
Kinematics of pure rolling without slipping: v_cm = ω R and a_cm = α R
Total kinetic energy in pure rolling: K = K_trans + K_rot = 1/2 M v_cm² + 1/2 I_cm ω² = 1/2 M v_cm² (1 + k²/R²)
Acceleration of rolling body down an inclined plane: a = (g sin θ) / (1 + k²/R²)
Minimum coefficient of friction required for pure rolling: μ_min = [tan θ · (k²/R²)] / [1 + (k²/R²)]

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 6: SYSTEM OF PARTICLES AND ROTATIONAL MOTION
## MODULE 6: Moment of Inertia, Theorems & Pure Rolling

### 1. Moment of Inertia ($I$) & Radius of Gyration ($k$)
- **Moment of Inertia**: The rotational analogue of mass in linear motion. It measures the body's inertia against angular acceleration.
  $$I = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i r_i^2 = \int r^2 dm$$
  where $r$ is the perpendicular distance of the mass element $dm$ from the chosen axis of rotation.
  - **SI Unit**: $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$.
  - **Dimensions**: $[M L^2 T^0]$.
- **Radius of Gyration ($k$)**: The distance from the axis of rotation at which the entire mass $M$ of the body could be concentrated without altering its moment of inertia:
  $$I = M k^2 \implies k = \sqrt{\frac{I}{M}}$$

### 2. Theorems of Moment of Inertia
1. **Perpendicular Axis Theorem** (Applies strictly to planar laminae in the xy-plane):
   $$I_z = I_x + I_y$$
2. **Parallel Axis Theorem** (Applies to any body of arbitrary shape):
   $$I = I_{\text{cm}} + M d^2$$
   where $I_{\text{cm}}$ is the moment of inertia about a parallel axis passing through the center of mass, and $d$ is the perpendicular distance between the two axes.

### 3. Standard Moments of Inertia Table
| Body | Axis of Rotation | Moment of Inertia ($I$) | $k^2 / R^2$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Thin Circular Ring** | Central axis $\perp$ to plane | $M R^2$ | $1$ |
| **Thin Circular Ring** | Diameter axis | $\frac{1}{2} M R^2$ | $1/2$ |
| **Circular Disc** | Central axis $\perp$ to plane | $\frac{1}{2} M R^2$ | $1/2$ |
| **Circular Disc** | Diameter axis | $\frac{1}{4} M R^2$ | $1/4$ |
| **Solid Cylinder** | Longitudinal axis | $\frac{1}{2} M R^2$ | $1/2$ |
| **Hollow Cylinder** | Longitudinal axis | $M R^2$ | $1$ |
| **Solid Sphere** | Any diameter axis | $\frac{2}{5} M R^2$ | $2/5 = 0.4$ |
| **Hollow Sphere (Shell)** | Any diameter axis | $\frac{2}{3} M R^2$ | $2/3 \approx 0.67$ |
| **Thin Rod (Length $L$)** | $\perp$ to rod at center | $\frac{1}{12} M L^2$ | $k^2 = L^2/12$ |
| **Thin Rod (Length $L$)** | $\perp$ to rod at one end | $\frac{1}{3} M L^2$ | $k^2 = L^2/3$ |

### 4. Mechanics of Pure Rolling Motion (Without Slipping)
- A body of radius $R$ rolling on a stationary surface undergoes simultaneous translation of center of mass and rotation about the center of mass.
  - Condition for rolling without slipping at point of contact: $v_{\text{contact}} = v_{\text{cm}} - \omega R = 0 \implies v_{\text{cm}} = \omega R$.
  - Acceleration relation: $a_{\text{cm}} = \alpha R$.
- **Total Kinetic Energy**:
  $$K = K_{\text{trans}} + K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} M v_{\text{cm}}^2 + \frac{1}{2} I_{\text{cm}} \omega^2 = \frac{1}{2} M v_{\text{cm}}^2 + \frac{1}{2} (M k^2) \left(\frac{v_{\text{cm}}}{R}\right)^2$$
  $$K = \frac{1}{2} M v_{\text{cm}}^2 \left(1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$$
- **Acceleration Down an Inclined Plane of Angle $\theta$**:
  $$a = \frac{g \sin \theta}{1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}}$$
- **Velocity at Bottom of Incline of Height $h$**:
  $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}}}$$
- **The Great Race Down the Incline**:
  Smaller $\frac{k^2}{R^2}$ means greater acceleration and velocity!
  $$\text{Solid Sphere } \left(\frac{k^2}{R^2} = 0.4\right) > \text{Disc } (0.5) > \text{Hollow Sphere } (0.67) > \text{Ring } (1.0)$$
  *The solid sphere always wins the race, and the ring arrives last!*

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 6.9: What is the moment of inertia of a disc of mass M and radius R about any of its diameter?
worked_examples.given: Circular disc of mass M, radius R.
worked_examples.formula: Perpendicular Axis Theorem: I_z = I_x + I_y. By symmetry, moments of inertia about any two perpendicular diameters in the plane are identical: I_x = I_y = I_d. Known: I_z = 1/2 M R².
worked_examples.substitution: I_z = I_d + I_d = 2 I_d ⇒ 2 I_d = 1/2 M R².
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The moment of inertia of a circular disc about any diameter is 1/4 M R².

worked_examples.problem: Textbook Example 6.10: What is the moment of inertia of a uniform rod of mass M and length L about an axis perpendicular to the rod and passing through one of its ends?
worked_examples.given: Uniform rod of mass M, length L. COM is at midpoint (d = L/2). Known: I_cm = 1/12 M L².
worked_examples.formula: Parallel Axis Theorem: I = I_cm + M d².
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The moment of inertia about an end perpendicular axis is 1/3 M L².

common_misconceptions: Assuming rolling friction does work against the kinetic energy of a rolling body: In pure rolling without slipping, the instantaneous contact point is at rest relative to the ground (v_contact = 0). Thus static friction does zero work! It merely enforces the constraint v_cm = ω R.

questions.question: A solid cylinder and a hollow cylinder of identical mass and radius are rolled down an inclined plane from rest. Which one reaches the bottom first?
questions.ideal_answer: The solid cylinder reaches first! Its moment of inertia is smaller (I = 1/2 M R², k²/R² = 0.5) compared to the hollow cylinder (I = M R², k²/R² = 1.0). Acceleration is a = (g sin θ) / (1 + k²/R²), so the solid cylinder has acceleration a = 2/3 g sin θ while the hollow cylinder has only a = 1/2 g sin θ.
questions.socratic_hint: Compare the k²/R² values for solid vs hollow cylinders.

chapter_notes:
# CHAPTER 6: SYSTEM OF PARTICLES AND ROTATIONAL MOTION
## MODULE 7: Master NCERT Exercise Solver (Ex 6.1 to 6.21)

### NCERT Exercise Solutions Overview
This module contains complete, board-exam compliant solutions for all 21 exercise problems from NCERT Chapter 6: System of Particles and Rotational Motion.
- **Exercises 6.1 - 6.3**: Geometric symmetry of center of mass, molecular diatomic centers of mass.
- **Exercises 6.4 - 6.7**: Angular kinematics, RPM to rad/s conversions, vector cross product identities.
- **Exercises 6.8 - 6.11**: Rigid body static equilibrium, levers, weighing scales, and ladder reaction forces.
- **Exercises 6.12 - 6.16**: Moments of inertia using parallel and perpendicular axis theorems.
- **Exercises 6.17 - 6.21**: Pure rolling on horizontal and inclined planes, energy partition ratios.

worked_examples.problem: NCERT Exercise 6.1: Give the location of the centre of mass of a (i) sphere, (ii) cylinder, (iii) ring, and (iv) cube, each of uniform mass density. Does the centre of mass of a body necessarily lie inside the body?
worked_examples.given: Four geometric bodies of uniform mass density.
worked_examples.formula: By symmetry principles, for any body of uniform density with geometric symmetry, the center of mass coincides with its geometric center.
worked_examples.substitution: (i) Sphere: At the geometric center of the sphere. (ii) Cylinder: At the midpoint of the longitudinal central axis of the cylinder. (iii) Ring: At the geometric center of the ring. (iv) Cube: At the point of intersection of the body diagonals of the cube.
worked_examples.calculation: No, the center of mass does not necessarily lie inside the body. In the case of a ring, hollow cylinder, hollow sphere, or hollow box, the center of mass lies in empty space where there is no physical material!
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (i) Geometric center; (ii) Midpoint of axis; (iii) Geometric center; (iv) Center of cube. The COM does NOT necessarily lie inside the material of the body (e.g. ring).

worked_examples.problem: NCERT Exercise 6.2: In the HCl molecule, the separation between the nuclei of the two atoms is about 1.27 Å (1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m). Find the approximate location of the CM of the molecule, given that a chlorine atom is about 35.5 times as massive as a hydrogen atom and nearly all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus.
worked_examples.given: d = 1.27 Å, m_H = 1 unit, m_Cl = 35.5 units.
worked_examples.formula: Taking hydrogen atom as origin (x_H = 0): X_cm = (m_H x_H + m_Cl x_Cl) / (m_H + m_Cl) = (m_Cl · d) / (m_H + m_Cl).
worked_examples.calculation: X_cm ≈ 1.24 Å from the hydrogen atom.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The center of mass of the HCl molecule is located approximately 1.24 Å from the hydrogen nucleus (or 0.035 Å from the chlorine nucleus).

common_misconceptions: Thinking that center of mass is equidistant between two particles: The center of mass is strictly weighted by mass! In HCl, because chlorine is 35.5 times heavier than hydrogen, the center of mass is situated right next to the chlorine atom (over 97% of the distance toward Cl)!

questions.question: What percentage of total kinetic energy is rotational for a uniform solid sphere rolling without slipping on a horizontal floor?
questions.ideal_answer: Approximately 28.6% (2/7 of total). For a solid sphere, K_rot = 1/2 I ω² = 1/2 (2/5 M R²) (v/R)² = 1/5 M v². K_trans = 1/2 M v². Total K = 1/2 M v² + 1/5 M v² = 7/10 M v². Fraction rotational = (1/5) / (7/10) = 2/7 ≈ 28.57%!

description: Historical transition from geocentric (Ptolemy) to heliocentric (Copernicus) models, Tycho Brahe's precision observational data, Johannes Kepler's three empirical laws of planetary motion, law of areas from angular momentum conservation, and deduction of Newton's inverse-square gravitational force.

Tycho Brahe's astronomical observations and Johannes Kepler's mathematical formulation
Kepler's First Law (Law of Orbits): All planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus
Geometry of an ellipse: Semi-major axis (a), semi-minor axis (b), eccentricity (e), perihelion, and aphelion
Kepler's Second Law (Law of Areas): The line joining the planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time
Derivation of Areal Velocity: dA/dt = 1/2 r² (dθ/dt) = L / (2m) = constant (conservation of angular momentum under central force)
Consequences of Law of Areas: Planet moves fastest at perihelion (closest to Sun) and slowest at aphelion (farthest)
Kepler's Third Law (Law of Periods): The square of the orbital period T is proportional to the cube of semi-major axis a (T² ∝ a³)
Deduction of Newton's inverse-square law: F = m v² / r = m (2π r / T)² / r = 4π² m r / T² = 4π² m r / (k r³) = (4π² m / k) (1 / r²)

Kepler's Third Law: Harmonic Law T² ∝ a³
